1. Executive Summary

We tested whether rain patterns during the planting window (April 1 – June 15) and harvest window (September 15 – November 30) predict yield losses in 10 Illinois farm counties, and whether Kalshi's rain contracts could offset those losses.

Largest payout in 45 years, correctly triggered by record wet spring
Key surprise: Rainfall basis risk is much lower for planting/harvest windows than for July. Our earlier heat study found July precipitation correlation averaging only r = 0.46 between Midway and farm counties. But for the longer planting and harvest windows (76 and 77 days), correlations average r = 0.85+. Longer windows smooth out daily storm randomness, making station-based rain contracts more viable than expected.

2. Why Off-Season Rain Matters

Farmers don't just worry about summer drought. Two other weather windows can make or break a crop year:

Planting Season (April 1 – June 15)

  • Corn must be planted by mid-May for optimal yields; soybeans by early June.
  • Fields must be dry enough to support heavy equipment — typically needing 1–2 dry days after rain.
  • A run of 5+ consecutive wet days can push planting back a full week, with every day of delay after May 15 costing roughly 1 bushel/acre in corn yield.
  • 2019 was the poster child: record spring rain across Illinois left millions of acres unplanted. USDA declared the largest prevented-planting event in decades.

Harvest Season (September 15 – November 30)

  • Wet fields delay combines, leading to late harvest, higher grain moisture (expensive drying), and risk of ear rot and stalk lodging.
  • A wet October can force farmers to choose between harvesting at high moisture (costly) or waiting and risking a November freeze.
  • 2009 was a classic late harvest: persistent fall rain pushed harvest well into November across much of Illinois.

The key insight: runs of consecutive wet days matter more than total rainfall. A 3-inch rain followed by 5 dry days is manageable; 10 days of 0.3-inch drizzle that never lets fields dry is devastating.

5. Which Rain Patterns Hurt Farmers Most?

We correlated each wet-spell metric with detrended corn and soybean yields across 45 years. To guard against overfitting, we split the data into even-year (train) and odd-year (test) halves.

Figure 3 — Ranking of planting-season rain metrics by correlation with corn yield. No single metric achieves strong statistical significance, but the direction is consistent: more rain / fewer workable days = lower yields.
Figure 4 — Scatter plots showing planting and harvest weather vs yield deviations. 2019, 1993, and 2009 are labeled where visible. The relationships are noisy but directionally correct.
Honest finding: Individual spring rain metrics are weak predictors of final yields. No single metric explains more than ~5% of corn yield variation. This doesn't mean rain doesn't matter — it means that spring rain primarily affects planting timing and prevented acreage, while final yields on acres that DO get planted are more affected by summer weather. The economic damage from wet springs is real but shows up in prevented planting and planting delays, not directly in per-acre yield numbers.

The harvest window similarly shows weak yield correlations — because harvest rain mainly increases drying costs and quality losses (mold, lodging), which aren't captured in yield-per-acre data.

This is a critical distinction: Kalshi rain contracts could still be valuable hedges, but the loss channel is prevented planting / delayed operations / quality degradation, not primarily yield-per-acre reductions.

6. Tipping Points

Figure 5 — Binned analysis showing average yield deviation by longest wet run (left) and by number of rain days (right). There is a suggestive pattern where yields drop once the longest wet spell exceeds ~7 days or rain days exceed ~25, but the sample sizes per bin are small. These tipping points should be treated as directional signals, not firm thresholds.

The data suggests a possible tipping point around 7+ consecutive wet days in the planting window, where yield impacts start becoming consistent. However, with only ~45 years of data and small bin sizes, this is a signal to watch rather than a confident threshold.

7. Basis Risk: Airport Rain vs Farm Rain

A critical question: if you buy a Kalshi rain contract settled at Midway Airport, does that actually reflect what happened on farms 40–80 miles away?

Figure 6 — Station rainfall vs county average for the planting window. Correlations range from 0.75 to 0.97. Springfield–Sangamon (r = 0.97) is remarkably tight. 2019 is labeled as the extreme wet year.

Much better than expected. Rainfall basis risk over 76-day windows (planting season) is dramatically lower than for single months. The longer averaging period smooths out daily storm randomness. All station–county pairs exceed r = 0.75, and most are above 0.85. This means station-settled Kalshi rain contracts are more usable for seasonal hedging than our earlier July-only analysis suggested.

8. Kalshi Rain Contract Rules

Based on current Kalshi offerings (late 2026):

Daily Rain Contracts

DetailChicagoNotes
Contract typeBinary: "Will it rain today?"Yes/No, pays $1.00 or $0.00
Settlement stationMidway (KMDW) for daily temp; O'Hare (KORD) for monthly rainCheck current rules — this has changed
Rain thresholdTypically ≥ 0.01" (any measurable)Trace (T) counts as 0.00"
Data sourceNWS Daily Climate Report / The Weather CompanyChanged Aug 2026
Listing horizon~7 days aheadForecast is partly known at purchase
Fair price (planting season)~$0.3939% of spring days have measurable rain

Monthly Rain Total Contracts

DetailValue
ThresholdsAbove 1", 2", 3", 4", 5", 6" etc.
Settlement stationO'Hare (KORD) as of Sep 2026
Cities available30+ cities — check for Chicago, St. Louis, Indianapolis
SpringfieldNot confirmed for Springfield IL specifically — may be Springfield MO or not available. Verify before trading.
Timing limitation: Daily rain contracts list only ~7 days before the event, when weather forecasts are already partially known. This means you're not buying pure "rain risk" — you're buying at prices that already reflect the forecast. A farmer who wants to hedge the entire planting season needs to buy contracts rolling, day by day, paying whatever the market charges once forecasts become available. The hedge is less about predicting rain and more about monetizing known rainy days that will prevent fieldwork.

9. Hedge Backtest: Three Strategies

We tested three approaches using a model farm: 600 acres corn + 400 acres soybeans, gross revenue $782,000 at trend yields.

Strategy A
Every Day
Buy 200 "rain YES" contracts for every day in the planting window (76 days)
Strategy B
Conditional
Buy "rain YES" only after 2+ consecutive wet days (bet the spell continues)
Strategy C
Monthly Total
Buy "above 4 inches" monthly contracts for Apr, May, Sep, Oct

10. Strategy Ranking

RankStrategyAvg Net/Year2019 NetAnnual CostComplexityVerdict

Strategy B has a genuine statistical edge. After 2+ consecutive wet days, the probability of rain on the next day jumps from 39% to 46% at Midway. If Kalshi prices daily rain contracts at the unconditional ~39% probability, buying selectively after wet spells produces a positive expected value. However, this edge may shrink if Kalshi's market makers start pricing persistence into their quotes.

11. Key Findings

Finding 1: Spring rain affects planting operations more than final yields

Individual rain metrics explain less than 5% of corn yield variation — but this understates the real economic impact. Wet springs cause prevented planting, delayed planting, and replanting costs that don't show up in yield-per-acre data. The 2019 prevented planting disaster confirms the economic harm is real, even if per-acre yields don't fully capture it.

Finding 2: Rainfall basis risk is manageable over multi-week windows

Station-to-county rainfall correlations average r = 0.85+ over the 76-day planting window — dramatically better than the r = 0.46 we found for July monthly rain. Longer windows smooth out the daily storm randomness that plagues single-day or single-month comparisons. Springfield–Sangamon reaches an exceptional r = 0.97.

Finding 3: Consecutive wet days matter — and are predictable

When it's been raining for 2+ days, the chance of rain continuing rises from 39% to 46% at Midway. This persistence creates a small but real trading edge if Kalshi prices contracts at unconditional probabilities. Strategy B exploits this.

Finding 4: Monthly rain contracts are the most practical starting point

Strategy C (monthly "above 4 inches" contracts for Apr/May/Sep/Oct) costs only ~$674/year and paid out $1,326 net in 2019. It requires no daily management, no conditional logic, and uses a contract type that Kalshi already offers for Chicago.

Finding 5: All three strategies produce modest, not transformative, payouts

Even in the worst year (2019), the best strategy pays out under $3,000 on a $782,000 farm. That's real money but it's less than 0.5% of gross revenue. These hedges are supplemental layers, not substitutes for crop insurance or prevented-planting coverage.

12. Limitations & Next Steps

Limitations

  • Yield data is estimated. NASS API was unavailable; county yields are derived from published state averages with county offsets. Real county data would sharpen the correlations.
  • No real Crop Progress data. USDA's weekly "percent planted" and "days suitable for fieldwork" data would be the ideal outcome variable. This is the single biggest data gap.
  • No prevented-planting acre data. FSA prevented-planting data by county would directly quantify the most important loss channel for wet springs.
  • No real Kalshi price history. We used historical frequency as the fair price. Actual Kalshi bid/ask spreads and market prices may differ — daily rain contracts that list only 7 days out are priced with forecast information already baked in.
  • Small sample sizes. Only ~45 years of data, with perhaps 5–8 truly "wet" years. Results should be treated as directional, not precise.
  • No drying-cost proxy. Harvest-season losses through higher grain moisture and propane drying costs are real but we could not quantify them without propane price and harvest-moisture data.

Next Steps

  1. Get a free NASS API key (quickstats.nass.usda.gov/api) and re-run with real county yields and Crop Progress data.
  2. Obtain FSA prevented-planting data — this would let us directly measure the spring-rain → lost-acres pathway.
  3. Collect actual Kalshi rain contract prices for 2024–2026 to compare fair-value estimates vs. market prices.
  4. Test multi-station portfolio hedges — buying rain contracts in both Chicago AND Springfield/Peoria to cover north + central IL simultaneously.
  5. Monitor Kalshi for new products — seasonal accumulation contracts (e.g., "total April-May rain days above 30") would be far more useful than daily binaries for farm hedging.
